blocks.content: The previous topic covered how a primary key uniquely identifies each row within its own table, a foreign key takes that identifier and uses it inside a different table, creating an enforced link between the two.

This topic covers exactly what a foreign key constraint enforces, what happens when a referenced row is deleted, and why this single feature is what keeps related data across separate tables from silently drifting out of sync.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438514304-302780702.png
1. What a Foreign Key Actually Is
blocks.text: 1. What a Foreign Key Actually Is

blocks.content: A foreign key is a column in one table that holds a value matching the primary key of a row in another table, this is the mechanism that lets an orders table say exactly which customer placed each order, without duplicating that customer full information into every single order row.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438514304-741176075.png
blocks.alt: What a Foreign Key Actually Is

blocks.content: 2. The Constraint the Database Actually Enforces
blocks.text: 2. The Constraint the Database Actually Enforces

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438514304-324664907.png
blocks.alt: The Constraint the Database Actually Enforces

blocks.content: Suppose you try to insert an order row with a customer_id of 99, if a foreign key constraint is declared and no customer with id 99 exists, the database rejects the insert outright, this is enforced automatically, an application never has to manually check this itself.

Declaring a foreign key constraint
3. What Happens When a Referenced Row Is Deleted
blocks.text: 3. What Happens When a Referenced Row Is Deleted

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438514305-819128662.png
blocks.alt: What Happens When a Referenced Row Is Deleted

blocks.content: Without any further instruction, deleting a customer that still has orders pointing to it would leave those orders referencing a customer_id that no longer exists, a genuinely broken state called an orphaned row, this is exactly the kind of silent inconsistency a foreign key constraint exists to prevent.
4. The Three Common Delete Behaviors
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438514305-389764891.png

A foreign key constraint can specify what should happen to referencing rows when the referenced row is deleted, CASCADE deletes the referencing rows too, RESTRICT blocks the delete entirely while any reference still exists, and SET NULL clears the foreign key column instead of deleting the referencing row.

{"headers":["Delete Behavior","What Happens to Referencing Rows"],"rows":[["CASCADE","Automatically deleted along with the referenced row"],["RESTRICT","The delete itself is blocked while any reference exists"],["SET NULL","The foreign key column is set to null, the row itself stays"]]}
5. Choosing the Right Delete Behavior

CASCADE makes sense when the referencing rows genuinely have no meaning without the parent, order line items without their order for instance, RESTRICT makes sense when losing the referencing data would be a serious mistake, and SET NULL fits cases where the relationship is optional to begin with.

blocks.title: CASCADE deletes can quietly remove more than expected
blocks.content: A CASCADE delete chain, especially across several linked tables, can remove far more data than a team initially expects, this behavior deserves careful, explicit review rather than being chosen as a default out of convenience.
6. A Foreign Key Represents a Real Relationship
blocks.text: 6. A Foreign Key Represents a Real Relationship

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438514305-279340859.png
blocks.alt: A Foreign Key Represents a Real Relationship

blocks.content: Each order row references exactly one customer row through its foreign key, this specific shape, many orders pointing to one customer, is a one to many relationship, the general topic of relationships between tables is covered in full in a later topic in this module.
7. Chains of Foreign Keys Across Multiple Tables
blocks.text: 7. Chains of Foreign Keys Across Multiple Tables

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438514550-59510013.png
blocks.alt: Chains of Foreign Keys Across Multiple Tables

blocks.content: Foreign keys often chain across more than two tables, a payments table might reference an order, which itself references a customer, this chain is exactly what makes a join, covered in the earlier SQL Joins module, able to reconstruct a full picture spanning customer, order, and payment in a single query.

blocks.title: A chain of foreign keys is what a multi table join actually traverses
blocks.content: When a query joins customers, orders, and payments together, it is literally following the foreign key chain linking those three tables, a join query and a foreign key relationship describe the same underlying structure from two different angles.
8. Common Mistakes
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438514551-840520695.png

["Skipping the foreign key constraint entirely and relying on application code alone to keep references consistent","Choosing CASCADE without fully considering how far the deletion chain could actually reach","Forgetting that a foreign key column needs an index for joins against it to stay fast, a concern covered further in the Indexing module","Assuming a foreign key column must have the exact same name as the primary key it references, when it only needs to match in type and value"]
items: Skipping the foreign key constraint entirely and relying on application code alone to keep references consistent
Choosing CASCADE without fully considering how far the deletion chain could actually reach
Forgetting that a foreign key column needs an index for joins against it to stay fast, a concern covered further in the Indexing module
Assuming a foreign key column must have the exact same name as the primary key it references, when it only needs to match in type and value

blocks.content: 9. Key Takeaways

["A foreign key column holds a value that must match a primary key value in another table, enforced directly by the database","CASCADE, RESTRICT, and SET NULL each define a different, explicit answer to what happens when the referenced row is deleted","Foreign keys chained across multiple tables are exactly what a join reconstructs during a query","The next topic, Candidate and Composite Keys, covers what happens when more than one column, or combination of columns, could serve as a unique identifier"]
items: A foreign key column holds a value that must match a primary key value in another table, enforced directly by the database
CASCADE, RESTRICT, and SET NULL each define a different, explicit answer to what happens when the referenced row is deleted
Foreign keys chained across multiple tables are exactly what a join reconstructs during a query
The next topic, Candidate and Composite Keys, covers what happens when more than one column, or combination of columns, could serve as a unique identifier
